claims.text: Controlled post-fabrication thermal annealing induces nanoscale chemical ordering in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Annealing-induced nanoscale ordered regions act as defect sinks.
The annealing-induced ordered regions enhance radiation tolerance in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The annealing intervention preserves mechanical integrity.
Conventionally processed TaNbHfZr or a similar refractory HEA has a random solid-solution initial state in the absence of deliberate ordering.
Heating near but below the alloy's recrystallization temperature can produce nanoscale compositional ordering.
The range 773–973 K represents reactor-relevant treatment and irradiation-test temperatures for fusion plasma-facing components.
Nanoscale ordered regions serve as recombination centers for irradiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Enhanced vacancy–interstitial recombination reduces irradiation-induced void formation.
Enhanced point-defect recombination reduces the formation and growth of detrimental defect clusters.
Annealed samples will have lower void density than unannealed samples after equivalent irradiation.
Annealed samples will have smaller irradiation-induced defect clusters than unannealed samples.
Annealed samples will retain or improve yield strength and other mechanical properties relative to the unannealed baseline after irradiation.
An irradiated random-solid-solution refractory HEA develops larger or more numerous defect clusters and more pronounced degradation than the proposed annealed state.
Over-aging or undesirable phase transformations can eliminate the proposed benefit.
Simulation and experimental evidence support formation of defect sinks through thermal annealing.
The quantitative radiation-tolerance improvement and optimal annealing parameters are not yet established.
